claim: C. elegans and P. pacificus shared their last common ancestor around 100 million years ago.
source: The species shared their last common ancestor around 100 million years ago, which is longer than the human-mouse separation (Nei et al., 2001; Prabh et al., 2018; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Werner et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research establishing the divergence time

claim: The divergence time between C. elegans and P. pacificus is longer than the human-mouse separation.
source: The species shared their last common ancestor around 100 million years ago, which is longer than the human-mouse separation (Nei et al., 2001; Prabh et al., 2018; Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013; Werner et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations comparing evolutionary divergence times

claim: C. elegans is a free-living nematode that can mainly be found in rotten fruit.
source: C. elegans is a free-living nematode that can mainly be found in rotten fruit while members of the genus Pristionchus are regularly found in association with several species of scarab beetles, depending on geography (Herrmann et al., 2006; Herrmann et al., 2007; Koneru et al., 2016; Ragsdale, 2015).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about C. elegans habitat and cited references

claim: Members of the genus Pristionchus are regularly found in association with several species of scarab beetles.
source: C. elegans is a free-living nematode that can mainly be found in rotten fruit while members of the genus Pristionchus are regularly found in association with several species of scarab beetles, depending on geography (Herrmann et al., 2006; Herrmann et al., 2007; Koneru et al., 2016; Ragsdale, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting Pristionchus-beetle associations

claim: Pristionchus nematodes are found in association with millipedes.
source: Additionally, Pristionchus nematodes are found in association with other soil arthropods, such as millipedes (Yoshida et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Pristionchus nematodes are found in insect baits for soil-dwelling entomopathogenic nematodes.
source: Pristionchus nematodes are found in association with other soil arthropods, such as millipedes (Yoshida et al., 2018) and insect baits for soil-dwelling entomopathogenic nematodes (Campos-Herrera et al., 2019; Kanzaki et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Pristionchus nematodes are found in vegetal substrates.
source: as well as other vegetal substrates (Félix et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Pristionchus nematodes exhibit chemosensory responses towards insect pheromones and volatile plant compounds.
source: First, Pristionchus nematodes exhibit chemosensory responses towards insect pheromones and volatile plant compounds (Hong and Sommer, 2006; Hong et al., 2008; Cinkornpumin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research demonstrating chemosensory responses

claim: P. pacificus dauer larvae secrete a high molecular weight wax ester that promotes collective host finding.
source: Second, P. pacificus dauer larvae secrete a high molecular weight wax ester that promotes collective host finding (Penkov et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Pristionchus species show predatory behavior towards C. elegans and other nematodes.
source: Finally, Pristionchus species show predatory behavior towards C. elegans and other nematodes (Bento et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research documenting predatory behavior

claim: The amphid sensilla are the largest nematode chemosensory organs.
source: The amphid sensilla, comprised of a pair of bilaterally symmetrical sensilla in the head that are open to the external environment, are the largest nematode chemosensory organs (Bargmann, 2006; Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991; Bargmann et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to established research on nematode sensory anatomy

claim: In C. elegans, the anterior sensilla include the amphid sensilla, twelve inner and six outer labial neurons, and four cephalic neurons, along with their associated sheath and socket support cells.
source: In the model organism C. elegans, the anterior sensilla include the amphid sensilla, twelve inner and six outer labial neurons, and four cephalic neurons, along with their associated sheath and socket support cells (Ward et al., 1975; Ware et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational anatomical studies of C. elegans

claim: P. pacificus possesses 12 neurons per amphid sensillum.
source: Like C. elegans, P. pacificus possesses 12 neurons per amphid sensillum.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions described in the manuscript

claim: All amphid neurons and the amphid sheath cell in P. pacificus have their cell bodies in the lateral ganglion posterior to the nerve ring.
source: All amphid neurons and the amphid sheath cell (AMsh) in P. pacificus have their cell bodies in the lateral ganglion posterior to the nerve ring, which resembles the condition found in C. elegans and other nematodes.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions and comparison to other species

claim: P. pacificus has 13 cilia from 11 neurons in each amphid channel.
source: We counted 13 cilia (from 11 neurons) in each amphid channel in P. pacificus, compared to 10 cilia (from eight neurons) in the channel in C. elegans (Figure 1D–F, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by direct counting from TEM images and comparison to C. elegans

claim: C. elegans has 10 cilia from eight neurons in the amphid channel.
source: We counted 13 cilia (from 11 neurons) in each amphid channel in P. pacificus, compared to 10 cilia (from eight neurons) in the channel in C. elegans (Figure 1D–F, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to established C. elegans anatomy

claim: P. pacificus lacks neurons with winged dendritic morphology.
source: The greater number of ciliated endings in P. pacificus coincides with a conspicuous lack of neurons with winged dendritic morphology found in the C. elegans wing cells (AWx)
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions showing absence of wing-shaped cilia

claim: The AWA, AWB, AWC cellular homologs in P. pacificus do not display a characteristic 'wing'-shaped cilia morphology.
source: This indicates that the AWA, AWB, AWC cellular homologs in P. pacificus are among the 11 single or double ciliated neurons in the channel and, therefore, do not display a characteristic 'wing'-shaped cilia morphology.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all P. pacificus amphid neurons have cilia in the channel

claim: The only other known amphid neurons with elaborate dendritic processes resembling the AWA cells are found in the swine parasite, Oesophagostomum dentatum.
source: The only other known amphid neurons with elaborate dendritic processes resembling the AWA cells are found in the swine parasite, Oesophagostomum dentatum (Hoholm et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The absence of wing neurons in most nematodes contributes to the difficulty in assigning homology in the amphid neurons.
source: Because the wing neurons are the most morphologically distinct and best studied amphid neurons in C. elegans, their absence in most other nematodes contributes to the difficulty in assigning homology in the amphid neurons in these other nematode species (Ashton et al., 1995; Bumbarger et al., 2007a; Bumbarger et al., 2009; Li et al., 2001; Ward et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference about comparative anatomy challenges

claim: AM12 is the P. pacificus homolog of the C. elegans AFD neuron.
source: Taken altogether, we conclude that AM12 is the P. pacificus homolog of AFD.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of anatomical evidence including finger-like dendritic endings and cell body position

claim: The AM12 sensory ending is formed by a short cilium of about 1 µm length and a complex of 30–40 microvilli-like projections.
source: The sensory ending of the AM12 dendrite is formed by a short cilium of about 1 µm length (in C. elegans about 500 nm, see Figure 12A in Doroquez et al., 2014) and a complex of 30–40 microvilli-like projections branching off from the periciliary membrane compartment (PCMC)
evidence: Supported by direct observation and measurement from TEM images

claim: The C. elegans AFD cilium is about 500 nm in length.
source: The sensory ending of the AM12 dendrite is formed by a short cilium of about 1 µm length (in C. elegans about 500 nm, see Figure 12A in Doroquez et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The AM12 morphology strongly resembles the morphology of the AFD neurons responsible for thermosensation in C. elegans, A. caninum, and H. contortus.
source: which strongly resembles the morphology of the AFD neurons responsible for thermosensation in C. elegans, A. caninum, and H. contortus (Bhopale et al., 2001; Li et al., 2001; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on AFD morphology across species

claim: The AM12 cilium is fully embedded in the amphid sheath cell process and does not enter the lumen of the sheath cell or the amphid channel.
source: Similar to AFD endings in other species, the AM12 cilium is fully embedded in the amphid sheath cell process, does not enter the lumen of the sheath cell or the amphid channel and thus has no contact to the outside environment.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: The cell body of AM12(AFD) is the most anterior among the amphid neurons, located just ventral of the lateral mid-line.
source: We also observed that like in other species, the cell body of AM12(AFD) is the most anterior among the amphid neurons, located just ventral of the lateral mid-line (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions and comparison to other species

claim: The AM12 sensory ending is located in a part of the AMsh that is clearly posterior to the lumen into which the other amphid dendrites enter.
source: Nevertheless, there is a small difference compared to other species – the AM12 sensory ending is located in a part of the AMsh that is clearly posterior to the lumen into which the other amphid dendrites enter.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: AM7 is the likely homolog of C. elegans AWC based on axon projection patterns.
source: As the AM7 and AWC axons both cross the dorsal midline and terminate above the lateral midline, we regard them as homologs based on this singular feature
evidence: Supported by direct observation of axon trajectories from 3D reconstructions

claim: The C. elegans AWC axons cross the dorsal midline, overlap each other and terminate just before reaching the lateral midline.
source: Using the 3D reconstructions of amphid neurons from EM sections (specimen 107, 148; Figure 3A; Figure 3—videos 1–15), we first looked for P. pacificus neurons that might share another defining feature of the C. elegans AWC neurons: the AWC axons cross the dorsal midline, overlap each other and terminate just before reaching the lateral midline.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of C. elegans neuroanatomy

claim: AM6 is likely the homolog of the C. elegans ASG neuron based on short axon projections.
source: The P. pacificus AM6 is likely the homolog of the C. elegans ASG neuron because these counterparts have the unique property of short axon projections that do not project into the nerve ring much further than the lateral midline, terminating before the dorsal midline.
evidence: Supported by direct observation of unique axon projection patterns from 3D reconstructions

claim: AM2 is the likely homolog of the C. elegans ADL neuron based on unique axon entry into the nerve ring.
source: The P. pacificus AM2 is the likely homolog of the C. elegans ADL neuron because like in ADL, the AM2 axons are the only amphid sensory neurons that do not run through the amphidial commissure but enter the nerve ring directly from an anterior projection before branching in the dorsal-ventral direction, which is unique among all amphid neurons in both species (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by direct observation of unique axon trajectories from 3D reconstructions

claim: The P. pacificus AM5(ASE) axons do not cross each other at the dorsal midline, but rather terminate at the dorsal midline.
source: However, the P. pacificus AM5(ASE) axons do not cross each other at the dorsal midline, but rather terminate at the dorsal midline.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from 3D reconstructions

claim: P. pacificus ASEL and ASER make a small gap junction with each other at their termination points.
source: At their respective termination points P. pacificus, ASEL and ASER make a small gap junction with each other, like all but two amphid sensory neuron pairs do (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by direct observation of synaptic connectivity from TEM reconstructions

claim: In C. elegans no gap junctions are formed between the ASE neurons.
source: This apparent electrical coupling between the P. pacificus ASE homologs is notable because in C. elegans no such gap junctions are formed between the ASEs (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to established C. elegans connectome data

claim: The lack of electrical coupling between the C. elegans ASEL and ASER neurons is necessary to produce a physiological asymmetry between these neurons.
source: The consequent lack of electrical coupling between the C. elegans ASEL and ASER neurons has been found to be necessary to produce a physiological asymmetry between these neurons, such that both neurons are differentially activated by distinct sensory cues, that is their function is 'lateralized' ('left/right asymmetric') (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Ortiz et al., 2009; Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on ASE laterality

claim: Artificial establishment of gap junctions between the left and right C. elegans ASEs leads to loss of functional lateralization and changes in chemotaxis behavior.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that artificial establishment of gap junctions between the left and right C. elegans ASEs leads to loss of functional lateralization and changes in chemotaxis behavior (Rabinowitch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published experimental research

claim: The apparent coupling of ASEL and ASER in P. pacificus suggests that these two neurons are not functionally lateralized in P. pacificus.
source: The apparent coupling of ASEL and ASER in P. pacificus suggests that these two neurons are not functionally lateralized in P. pacificus.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of gap junctions and comparison to C. elegans functional studies

claim: The miRNA lsy-6 does not exist in the P. pacificus genome.
source: First, the key regulatory factor that triggers the asymmetry of the ASEL/R neurons in C. elegans, the miRNA lsy-6 (Cochella and Hobert, 2012; Johnston and Hobert, 2003), does not exist in the P. pacificus genome and is apparently specific to the Caenorhabditis crown clade (Ahmed et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published genomic analysis

claim: The miRNA lsy-6 is apparently specific to the Caenorhabditis crown clade.
source: First, the key regulatory factor that triggers the asymmetry of the ASEL/R neurons in C. elegans, the miRNA lsy-6 (Cochella and Hobert, 2012; Johnston and Hobert, 2003), does not exist in the P. pacificus genome and is apparently specific to the Caenorhabditis crown clade (Ahmed et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on miRNA evolution

claim: The ASEL and ASER neurons in C. elegans each express a different subfamily of duplicated and chromosomally-linked receptor-type guanylyl cyclases.
source: Second, the ASEL and ASER neurons in C. elegans (as well as closely related Caenorhabditis species) each express a different subfamily of duplicated and chromosomally-linked, receptor-type guanylyl cyclases (rGCYs), the ASER-rGCYs (e.g. gcy-1, gcy-2, gcy-3, gcy-4, gcy-5) and the ASEL-rGCYs (gcy-6, gcy-7, gcy-14, gcy-20) (Ortiz et al., 2006; Yu et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on ASE gene expression

claim: Several members of the C. elegans ASE-expressed rGCYs are thought to be salt chemoreceptors.
source: several members of which are thought to be salt chemoreceptors (Ortiz et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The P. pacificus genome contains no C. elegans-ASEL-type or ASER-type rGCYs.
source: In contrast, the P. pacificus genome contains no C. elegans- ASEL-type or ASER-type rGCYs (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: In C. elegans non-dauer hermaphrodites, DiI, DiO, and FITC routinely stain five specific pairs of amphid neurons - ASK, ADL, ASI, ASH, ASJ.
source: In C. elegans non-dauer hermaphrodites, DiI, DiO, and FITC routinely stain five specific pairs of amphid neurons with open sensory endings to the environment - ASK, ADL, ASI, ASH, ASJ (Table 3; Figure 4B and I) - along with two pairs of tail phasmid sensory neurons - PHA and PHB.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of C. elegans dye-filling patterns and citations

claim: In C. elegans, ADF is stained weakly by FITC but not by DiI.
source: Additionally, ADF is stained weakly by FITC but not by DiI, while AWB is stained weakly by DiI but more strongly by DiO (Hedgecock et al., 1985; Perkins et al., 1986; Starich et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on dye-filling patterns

claim: In C. elegans, AWB is stained weakly by DiI but more strongly by DiO.
source: Additionally, ADF is stained weakly by FITC but not by DiI, while AWB is stained weakly by DiI but more strongly by DiO (Hedgecock et al., 1985; Perkins et al., 1986; Starich et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on dye-filling patterns

claim: Cell ablations of the DiI positive ASH neurons show that its polymodal function is strongly conserved across various nematode species.
source: The cell ablations of the DiI positive ASH neurons show that its polymodal function is strongly conserved across various nematode species (Srinivasan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published functional studies

claim: In P. pacificus young adult hermaphrodites, DiI stains five pairs of amphid neurons: AM9, AM4, AM2(ADL), AM1, and AM8.
source: In P. pacificus young adult hermaphrodites, DiI stains five pairs of amphid neurons in a pattern similar to the one in C. elegans [AM9, AM4, AM2(ADL), AM1, and AM8] (n > 50; Figure 4A–B)
evidence: Supported by direct observation from dye-filling experiments

claim: In P. pacificus, DiO stains only the AM2(ADL) and AM8 neurons.
source: but DiO stains only the AM2(ADL) and AM8 neurons (Figures 4E, G and H; Table 3).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from dye-filling experiments

claim: The P. pacificus phasmid neurons only dye fill in the dauer larvae.
source: In contrast to C. elegans, the P. pacificus phasmid neurons only dye fill in the dauer larvae (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by direct observation from dye-filling experiments

claim: The P. pacificus AM11(AWB) neurons rarely dye fill in any developmental stage with either dye.
source: while the AM11(AWB) neurons rarely dye fill in any developmental stage with either dye (AWB is stained more robustly with DiO than with DiI in C. elegans).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from dye-filling experiments

claim: AM9 is nominated as the ADF homolog primarily due to the conservation of a distinctively bulbous PCMC similar to the C. elegans ADF.
source: In addition to the conservation in DiI staining, we have nominated AM9 as the ADF homolog primarily due to the conservation of a distinctively bulbous PCMC in the ultrastructure of the P. pacificus AM9 similar to the C. elegans ADF (Figure 1G–H) (Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images and comparison to published C. elegans data

claim: The putative ASI homolog, AM10, does not take up DiI.
source: In this proposed homology, the putative ASI homolog, AM10, does not take up DiI.
evidence: Inferred from the dye-filling pattern and homology assignments

claim: In C. elegans, the ASI neurons are important for regulating dauer development.
source: In C. elegans, the ASI neurons are important for regulating dauer development and are remodeled in the dauer larvae such that the dauer ASI neurons no longer take up DiI due to cilia retraction from the amphid pore (Albert and Riddle, 1983; Peckol et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on ASI function

claim: The dauer ASI neurons in C. elegans no longer take up DiI due to cilia retraction from the amphid pore.
source: In C. elegans, the ASI neurons are important for regulating dauer development and are remodeled in the dauer larvae such that the dauer ASI neurons no longer take up DiI due to cilia retraction from the amphid pore (Albert and Riddle, 1983; Peckol et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on dauer remodeling

claim: P. pacificus daf-6 expression shows strong conservation in the AMsh, excretory duct and pore, seam cells, and VulE epidermal cell.
source: Indeed, P. pacificus daf-6 expression shows strong conservation not only in the AMsh, but also in cells of the excretory duct and pore, seam cells, as well as in the VulE epidermal cell that contributes to vulva formation during the mid-J4 larval stage (Perens and Shaham, 2005) (Figure 6A; Figure 6—video 1; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from transgenic reporter expression

claim: The cell bodies of the amphid sheath cells in P. pacificus are distinctively large and sit dorso-anteriorly to the terminal bulb of the pharynx.
source: The cell bodies of the amphid sheath cells are distinctively large and sit dorso-anteriorly to the terminal bulb of the pharynx.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM and fluorescence imaging

claim: The P. pacificus AMsh cells extend thick processes anteriorly that swell to form vesicle-filled paddle-like endings near the nose of the worm.
source: The AMsh cells extend thick processes anteriorly that swell to form vesicle-filled paddle-like endings near the nose of the worm (Figure 2A–B, Figure 3A–B)
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: All non-finger amphid neurons in P. pacificus have dendritic processes that terminate in the amphid channel and are thus in direct contact to the external environment.
source: In contrast to C. elegans, all the non-finger amphid neurons in P. pacificus have dendritic processes that terminate in the amphid channel and are thus in direct contact to the external environment (Figure 1A–F, Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: The C. elegans amphid sheath cells can fuse to each other in the dauer larvae.
source: Because the C. elegans AMsh cells accommodate the prominently large AWC winged neurons, the left and the right AMsh can fuse to each other in the dauer larvae, which undergo radial constriction during dauer entry (Procko et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Ppa-daf-6p::rfp expression in the pair of anterior AMsh endings remains distinctively separated in P. pacificus dauer larvae.
source: Given the absence of any amphid neurons with winged morphology in P. pacificus, not surprisingly, Ppa-daf-6p::rfp expression in the pair of anterior AMsh endings remains distinctively separated in P. pacificus dauer larvae (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from transgenic reporter expression in dauer larvae

claim: The P. pacificus amphid sheath morphology is tubular, lacking the distal enlargement of the C. elegans amphid sheath.
source: As a result, the P. pacificus amphid sheath morphology is tubular, lacking the distal enlargement of the C. elegans amphid sheath.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of sheath morphology and comparison to C. elegans

claim: Recent studies using live imaging on a much larger number of C. elegans samples reveal some variability in dendrite entry during larval development.
source: However, recent studies using live imaging on a much larger number of C. elegans samples reveal some variability in dendrite entry during larval development (Yip and Heiman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The first dendrites to enter the P. pacificus amphid sheath are those of the finger neurons AM12(AFD) at approximately 25 µm from the tip of the head.
source: The first dendrites to enter are those of the finger neurons AM12(AFD) at approximately 25 µm from the tip of the head, or 1/6 the remaining distance between the posterior end of the pharynx (section 3000) and the tip of the 'nose' at the anterior end (Section 0).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM serial sections

claim: The sequence and site of entry for many neurons relative to the amphid sheath are variable in P. pacificus.
source: Thus, the sequence and site of entry for many neurons relative to the amphid sheath are variable in P. pacificus, but higher sample size involving semi-automated live imaging would be necessary to determine if the left-right variability is consistent and if the degree of variability is different between P. pacificus and C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM serial sections showing left-right differences

claim: The BAG neurons are required for CO2 and O2 sensing in C. elegans.
source: Of these, the BAG neurons (named for bag-like sensory ending) stand out for being required for CO2 and O2 sensing in C. elegans (Hallem and Sternberg, 2008; Zimmer et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to published functional studies

claim: The BAG neurons are required for CO2 avoidance in P. pacificus.
source: as well as CO2 avoidance in P. pacificus (Hallem et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to published functional study

claim: In P. pacificus, the two BAG neuron cell bodies are located just anterior of the nerve ring in subventral position close to the isthmus.
source: In P. pacificus, the two BAG neuron cell bodies are located just anterior of the nerve ring in subventral position close to the isthmus (Figure 3A–B, Figure 7A–B)
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: The ciliated distal ends of the BAG processes in P. pacificus form branched lamellae around the ventral halves of the lateral inner labial socket cells.
source: The ciliated distal ends of these processes form branched lamellae around the ventral halves of the lateral inner labial socket cells (ILsoL), opposite to those of another pair of internal receptors, the URX neurons (Figure 1L, Figure 7A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: The pair of URX neurons in C. elegans is known to be important for sensing oxygen levels and to control carbon dioxide response.
source: In C. elegans, the pair of URX neurons is known to be important for sensing oxygen levels and to control carbon dioxide response (Carrillo et al., 2013; Gray et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published functional studies

claim: The cell body of the URX neuron in both nematode species is located posterior to the nerve ring, and directly anterior to the anterior-most amphid neuron cell body in dorsal position.
source: The cell body of the URX neuron in both nematode species is located posterior to the nerve ring, and directly anterior to the anterior-most amphid neuron cell body in dorsal position [AM9(ADF) in P. pacificus and ASK in C. elegans] (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions and comparison to C. elegans

claim: The dendritic endings of the P. pacificus URX neurons appear to be ciliated with eight microtubules.
source: Interestingly, the dendritic endings of the homologous pair of P. pacificus URX neurons appear to be ciliated with eight microtubules, which are associated with the dorsal half of the lateral IL socket cells (Figure 1L, Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: The C. elegans URX neurons are non-ciliated and unaffiliated with any sensilla.
source: In contrast, the C. elegans URX neurons are non-ciliated and unaffiliated with any sensilla (Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Ciliated URX neurons are found in Acrobeles complexus.
source: Ciliated URX neurons are also found in other nematode species, for example, in one of two dendritic endings of the URX neurons in the soil-dwelling nematode Acrobeles complexus, as well as in all of the URX endings of the mycophagus nematode Aphelenchus avenae (Bumbarger et al., 2007b; Ragsdale et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published comparative studies

claim: Ciliated URX neurons are found in Aphelenchus avenae.
source: Ciliated URX neurons are also found in other nematode species, for example, in one of two dendritic endings of the URX neurons in the soil-dwelling nematode Acrobeles complexus, as well as in all of the URX endings of the mycophagus nematode Aphelenchus avenae (Bumbarger et al., 2007b; Ragsdale et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published comparative studies

claim: The four putative URY neurons in P. pacificus have dendritic endings with numerous (6-20) singlet microtubules but do not appear to be ciliated.
source: Similarly, the four putative URY neurons have dendritic endings with numerous (6-20) singlet microtubules but they do not appear to be ciliated.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: Wing neurons (AWx) and unciliated URX neurons are derived characters in C. elegans.
source: A comparison of C. elegans, P. pacificus, and A. complexus suggests that wing neurons (AWx) and unciliated URX neurons are derived characters in C. elegans, whereas ciliated BAG and unciliated URY are conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis across three species

claim: Ciliated BAG and unciliated URY are conserved characters across C. elegans, P. pacificus, and A. complexus.
source: A comparison of C. elegans, P. pacificus, and A. complexus suggests that wing neurons (AWx) and unciliated URX neurons are derived characters in C. elegans, whereas ciliated BAG and unciliated URY are conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis across three species

claim: The C. elegans FLP neurons have elaborate multi-dendritic structures throughout the head region.
source: The C. elegans FLP neurons have elaborate multi-dendritic structures throughout the head region, and are polymodal receptors for thermosensation and mechanosensation (Albeg et al., 2011; Chatzigeorgiou and Schafer, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on FLP function

claim: The cell bodies of the likely FLP homologs in P. pacificus are located posterior to all of the amphid neuron cell bodies near the terminal pharyngeal bulb.
source: Like in C. elegans, the cell bodies of the likely FLP homologs in P. pacificus are located posterior to all of the amphid neuron cell bodies near the terminal pharyngeal bulb and have dendrites with extensive branching, whereas their axon projections do not enter the nerve ring.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: The P. pacificus FLP neurons do not appear to be associated with the lateral IL socket cell.
source: Unlike the FLP neurons in C. elegans however, the P. pacificus FLP neurons do not appear to be associated with the lateral IL socket cell (Doroquez et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images and comparison to published C. elegans data

claim: In C. elegans, the BAG and FLP neurons are unusual among the anterior sensory neurons for not possessing their own set of glial cells.
source: In C. elegans, the BAG and FLP neurons are unusual among the anterior sensory neurons for not possessing their own set of glial cells, but instead associate with the socket cells of the lateral IL neurons (Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: AMU1 is the likely homolog of C. elegans AUA based on dendritic structural similarity and axonal projection.
source: Given this strong dendritic structural similarity, as well as a similar axonal projection, AMU1 is the likely homolog of AUA.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions showing conserved morphology

claim: The C. elegans AUA neurons mediate oxygen sensing and social feeding behavior.
source: The conservation of the AMU1(AUA) neurons, which mediate oxygen sensing and social feeding behavior in C. elegans, implies that they share conserved functions in several nematode species (Bumbarger et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2006; Coates and de Bono, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published functional studies

claim: Striking similarities in axonal placement were observed between P. pacificus and C. elegans in both the ventral ganglion and dorsal midline.
source: Despite differences in sample preparation (HPF for P. pacificus and chemical fixation for C. elegans) and EM section thickness (50 nm for P. pacificus and ~80 nm for C. elegans), we observed striking similarities in axonal placement in both species, providing further strong support for our homology assignment of neurons.
evidence: Supported by direct observation and comparison of TEM images from both species

claim: Similar amphid sensory neuron axonal fasciculation was observed along the ventrodorsal and mediolateral axes of the ventral ganglion in both species.
source: For example, we observed similar amphid sensory neuron axonal fasciculation along the ventrodorsal and mediolateral axes of the ventral ganglion, where the ASJ and ASG neurons are most lateral, and the AFD and AUA neurons are the most ventral in both species (Figure 8B and D).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: The most posterior segment of the dorsal nerve cord is occupied by a similar set of neurons in both P. pacificus and C. elegans.
source: The most posterior segment of the dorsal nerve cord, where most bilaterally symmetric neurons meet, is occupied by a similar set of neurons in both species (Figure 8C and E).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: The ASJ neurons are most ventral in both P. pacificus and C. elegans at the dorsal midline.
source: Also, of note are the ASJ neurons, which are most ventral, and ADL, which are most lateral in both P. pacificus and C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: The ADL neurons are most lateral in both P. pacificus and C. elegans at the dorsal midline.
source: Also, of note are the ASJ neurons, which are most ventral, and ADL, which are most lateral in both P. pacificus and C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images

claim: In C. elegans there are four first-layer amphid interneuron classes, each composed of a bilaterally symmetric pair of neurons (AIA, AIB, AIY, AIZ).
source: In C. elegans there are four such amphid interneuron classes, each composed of a bilaterally symmetric pair of neurons (termed AIA, AIB, AIY, AIZ, for Amphid Interneuron A, B, Y and Z).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of C. elegans neuroanatomy

claim: All four amphid interneuron classes display highly distinctive features that are remarkably conserved between P. pacificus and C. elegans.
source: All four neurons display highly distinctive features and an examination of the P. pacificus nervous system revealed a remarkable extent of conservation of these features, thereby easily identifying these neurons
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions showing conserved morphology

claim: In both species, the AIY interneuron cell bodies are located in the same relative position in the ventral ganglion.
source: In both species, the AIY interneuron cell bodies are located in the same relative position in the ventral ganglion and their axons display a characteristic 'humped' morphology (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions and comparison to published C. elegans data

claim: The AIY axons display a characteristic 'humped' morphology in both species.
source: In both species, the AIY interneuron cell bodies are located in the same relative position in the ventral ganglion and their axons display a characteristic 'humped' morphology (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions and comparison to published C. elegans data

claim: The 'humped' morphology of AIY corresponds to a large synaptic output onto AIZ.
source: This 'humped' morphology corresponds to a large synaptic output onto AIZ, which forms a sheet-like cross-section immediately dorsal to AIY (Figure 8B and D).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM images showing synaptic anatomy

claim: The AIB neurons are identifiable in both species by a characteristic switch of their process into two distinct neighborhoods of the anterior portion of the ventral ganglion.
source: The AIB neurons are identifiable in both species by a characteristic switch of their process into two distinct neighborhoods of the anterior portion of the ventral ganglion, where its proximal axon is ventral and its distal axon is more dorsal.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: The somas of the P. pacificus and C. elegans AIA interneurons occupy a stereotypic mediodorsal location.
source: The somas of the P. pacificus and C. elegans AIA interneurons occupy a stereotypic mediodorsal location and, like the AIY and AIZ neurons, form a dorsal midline gap junction.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: The AIA, AIY and AIZ neurons form a dorsal midline gap junction in both species.
source: The somas of the P. pacificus and C. elegans AIA interneurons occupy a stereotypic mediodorsal location and, like the AIY and AIZ neurons, form a dorsal midline gap junction.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: 138 chemical connections were identified in P. pacificus between amphid sensory neurons, AUA, and amphid interneurons.
source: We identified 138 chemical connections (directed edges in a graph of connectivity) and 98 gap junction connections (undirected edges) in P. pacificus, compared to 73 chemical edges and 96 gap junction edges in a recent re-evaluation of connectivity in C. elegans (Cook et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by direct annotation of synapses from TEM reconstructions

claim: 98 gap junction connections were identified in P. pacificus between amphid sensory neurons, AUA, and amphid interneurons.
source: We identified 138 chemical connections (directed edges in a graph of connectivity) and 98 gap junction connections (undirected edges) in P. pacificus, compared to 73 chemical edges and 96 gap junction edges in a recent re-evaluation of connectivity in C. elegans (Cook et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by direct annotation of synapses from TEM reconstructions

claim: 73 chemical edges were identified in C. elegans between amphid sensory neurons, AUA, and amphid interneurons in a recent re-evaluation.
source: We identified 138 chemical connections (directed edges in a graph of connectivity) and 98 gap junction connections (undirected edges) in P. pacificus, compared to 73 chemical edges and 96 gap junction edges in a recent re-evaluation of connectivity in C. elegans (Cook et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published connectome re-analysis

claim: 96 gap junction edges were identified in C. elegans between amphid sensory neurons, AUA, and amphid interneurons in a recent re-evaluation.
source: We identified 138 chemical connections (directed edges in a graph of connectivity) and 98 gap junction connections (undirected edges) in P. pacificus, compared to 73 chemical edges and 96 gap junction edges in a recent re-evaluation of connectivity in C. elegans (Cook et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published connectome re-analysis

claim: Of the strong chemical synaptic connections, 32/53 connections were present in both species.
source: Of these strong chemical synaptic connections, 32/53 connections were present in both species while 15 and 6 were specific to P. pacificus and C. elegans, respectively.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of synaptic connectivity data

claim: 15 strong chemical synaptic connections were specific to P. pacificus.
source: Of these strong chemical synaptic connections, 32/53 connections were present in both species while 15 and 6 were specific to P. pacificus and C. elegans, respectively.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of synaptic connectivity data

claim: 6 strong chemical synaptic connections were specific to C. elegans.
source: Of these strong chemical synaptic connections, 32/53 connections were present in both species while 15 and 6 were specific to P. pacificus and C. elegans, respectively.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of synaptic connectivity data

claim: Four of the strong gap junction connections were present in both species.
source: Four of the strong gap junction connections were present in both species while 6 and 2 were specific to P. pacificus and C. elegans, respectively (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of synaptic connectivity data

claim: 6 strong gap junction connections were specific to P. pacificus.
source: Four of the strong gap junction connections were present in both species while 6 and 2 were specific to P. pacificus and C. elegans, respectively (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of synaptic connectivity data

claim: 2 strong gap junction connections were specific to C. elegans.
source: Four of the strong gap junction connections were present in both species while 6 and 2 were specific to P. pacificus and C. elegans, respectively (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of synaptic connectivity data

claim: Conserved edges are larger and more frequently made by amphid interneurons.
source: We found that, on average, conserved edges are larger and more frequently made by amphid interneurons.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of connectivity patterns

claim: Neurons whose structure is qualitatively most similar between species made more similar synaptic outputs.
source: Moreover, neurons whose structure is qualitatively most similar between species made more similar synaptic outputs (Figure 9B).
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of structure and connectivity

claim: The synaptic output of AFD is almost exclusively onto AIY in both species.
source: Examples include the synaptic output of AFD, whose output is almost exclusively onto AIY
evidence: Supported by direct observation from connectivity analysis

claim: AWA makes strong synaptic connections to the AIB interneurons exclusively in P. pacificus.
source: For example, AWA makes strong synaptic connections to the AIB interneurons exclusively in P. pacificus.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from connectivity analysis

claim: The P. pacificus polymodal ASH neuron class makes P. pacificus-specific outputs to AIY and is innervated by AIA.
source: Similarly, the P. pacificus polymodal ASH neuron class makes P. pacificus-specific outputs to AIY and is innervated by AIA.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from connectivity analysis

claim: The AUA is presynaptic to the RIA and RIB interneurons in both species.
source: Similarly, the AUA is presynaptic to the RIA and RIB interneurons in both species.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from connectivity analysis

claim: The AUA neuron is the exclusive target of the ADF neurons in both species.
source: Like in C. elegans, the AUA neuron is the exclusive target of the ADF neurons.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from connectivity analysis

claim: Many of the P. pacificus-specific synaptic contacts concern the connection of sensory neurons to first layer interneurons.
source: While many of the P. pacificus-specific synaptic contacts concern the connection of sensory neurons to first layer interneurons, many of the C. elegans-specific synaptic contacts concern the connections between sensory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of connectivity patterns

claim: Many of the C. elegans-specific synaptic contacts concern the connections between sensory neurons.
source: While many of the P. pacificus-specific synaptic contacts concern the connection of sensory neurons to first layer interneurons, many of the C. elegans-specific synaptic contacts concern the connections between sensory neurons.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of connectivity patterns

claim: All 21 neuron-neuron pairs with species-specific connections make physical contact in both species.
source: Of the 29 species-specifc connections, there are only 21 pairs of possible neuron-neuron adjacencies due to reciprocal connectivity. Of these 21 neuron-neuron pairs, we found that all make physical contact in both species.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of neuronal adjacency

claim: Among species-specific neuronal partnerships, the percent of axonal-axonal contact ranged from 0.95% to 142% with a median contact of 26.7%.
source: Among species-specific neuronal partnerships, we found the percent of axonal-axonal contact ranged from 0.95% to 142% (median contact 26.7%) (Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of neuronal adjacency

claim: There is a very weak, non-significant correlation between synaptic connectivity and neuron-neuron adjacency in both species.
source: We compared the correlation between synaptic connectivity and neuron-neuron adjacency and found a very weak, non-significant, correlation in both species (Spearman's R = 0.2042, p=0.3747 in P. pacificus; Spearman's R = 0.1248, p=0.5898 in C. elegans).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of connectivity and adjacency data

claim: Species-specific differences in connectivity are largely determined by synaptic partnership choice or recognition rather than large differences in axonal fasciculation and neuronal neighborhood changes.
source: Together, these results suggest that species-specific differences in connectivity are largely determined by synaptic partnership choice or recognition rather than large differences in axonal fasciculation and neuronal neighborhood changes.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis showing weak correlation between adjacency and connectivity

claim: There appears to be a much smaller number of GPCR-type sensory receptor-encoding genes in P. pacificus compared to C. elegans.
source: For example, several censuses taken for the number of GPCR-type sensory receptor-encoding genes indicated a much smaller number in P. pacificus compared to C. elegans (Dieterich et al., 2008; Krishnan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published genomic analyses

claim: oig-8 encodes a single transmembrane, immunoglobulin domain protein that is not encoded in the P. pacificus genome.
source: oig-8 encodes a single transmembrane, immunoglobulin domain protein that not encoded in the P. pacificus genome.
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison and citation to published research

claim: Mis-expression of Cel-oig-8 under the Ppa-odr-7 promoter did not induce branching in P. pacificus neurons.
source: To assess whether this gene loss is responsible for the lack of winged cilia in P. pacificus, we mis-expressed Cel-oig-8 under the Ppa-odr-7 promoter (described below) along with the Ppa-odr-7p::rfp marker but found no difference in the terminal dendritic cilia of RFP positive neurons that were co-injected with the Ppa-odr-7p::Cel-oig-8 transgene compared to those that were injected only with the Ppa-odr-7p::RFP marker (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by direct experimental observation from transgenic analysis

claim: The two Ppa-odr-7-expressing amphid neurons may lack other factors involved in ciliary membrane morphogenesis in wing neurons.
source: This result suggests the two Ppa-odr-7-expressing amphid neurons may lack other factors (DiTirro et al., 2019), such as factors involved in ciliary membrane morphogenesis in wing neurons, to realize the branching function of Cel-oig-8﻿.
evidence: Inferred from the negative result of the oig-8 mis-expression experiment

claim: Ppa-che-1 is expressed in two neuronal pairs in the head region of P. pacificus.
source: We generated a reporter gene fusion for the Ppa-che-1 locus and found that transgenic P. pacificus expressed the reporter in two rather than one neuronal pairs in the head region of the worm (Figure 4E, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from transgenic reporter expression

claim: Ppa-che-1 is provisionally expressed in the AM5(ASE) and AM6(ASG) neurons based on cell positions and axon projections.
source: By cell positions, as well as by the axons meeting at the dorsal midline using fluorescence microscopy, we provisionally identified these neurons as the AM5(ASE) and, tentatively, the AM6(ASG) neurons.
evidence: Inferred from cell position and axon trajectory observations

claim: The ASG neuron in C. elegans is a water-soluble chemical taste receptor.
source: Expression in AM5(ASE) matches the expression observed in C. elegans and expression in AM6(ASG) is notable because the ASG neuron is also a water-soluble chemical taste receptor (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The ASG neuron can compensate for loss of ASE function under hypoxic conditions in C. elegans.
source: that can compensate for loss of ASE function under hypoxic conditions (Pocock and Hobert, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Ppa-odr-7p::rfp reporter is expressed in the proposed AM7(AWC) and AM9(ADF) neuron pairs based on cell body position and axonal projections.
source: Based on cell body position and axonal projections, a Ppa-odr-7p::rfp reporter is expressed in the proposed AM7(AWC) and AM9(ADF) neuron pairs (Figure 4G–H, Figure 4—video 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), but not in AM3(AWA), the exclusive expression site of odr-7 in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from transgenic reporter expression

claim: C. elegans odr-7 is exclusively expressed in AWA.
source: Based on cell body position and axonal projections, a Ppa-odr-7p::rfp reporter is expressed in the proposed AM7(AWC) and AM9(ADF) neuron pairs (Figure 4G–H, Figure 4—video 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), but not in AM3(AWA), the exclusive expression site of odr-7 in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of C. elegans gene expression

claim: C. elegans odr-7 contributes to the specification of the C. elegans-specific elaborations of the AWA cilia.
source: This divergence of expression is particularly notable if one considers that C. elegans odr-7 contributes to the specification of the C. elegans--specific elaborations of the AWA cilia (Howell and Hobert, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: P. pacificus AM3(AWA) does not express odr-7 and its cilia do not display the winged elaborations.
source: In contrast, P. pacificus AM3(AWA) does not express odr-7 and its cilia do not display the winged elaborations, as discussed above.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from reporter expression and TEM analysis

claim: The P. pacificus genome contains almost all of the downstream G-protein subunit signaling proteins found to be encoded in the C. elegans genome.
source: In contrast to the reduction of gcy genes important for C. elegans ASE laterality, the P. pacificus genome contains almost all of the downstream G-protein subunit signaling proteins found to be encoded in the C. elegans genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Ppa-odr-3p::rfp shows consistent expression in AM3(AWA) and less robust expression in AM4(ASK).
source: We found consistent Ppa-odr-3p::rfp expression in AM3(AWA) and less robust expression in AM4(ASK) (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by direct observation from transgenic reporter expression

claim: Neuronal number appears invariant between C. elegans and P. pacificus.
source: Neuron number appears invariant, neuronal soma position is restricted, and perhaps most remarkable are the similarities in process outgrowth and relative process position.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: Neuronal soma position is restricted between C. elegans and P. pacificus.
source: Neuron number appears invariant, neuronal soma position is restricted, and perhaps most remarkable are the similarities in process outgrowth and relative process position.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: There are remarkable similarities in process outgrowth and relative process position between C. elegans and P. pacificus.
source: Neuron number appears invariant, neuronal soma position is restricted, and perhaps most remarkable are the similarities in process outgrowth and relative process position.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: Relative neighborhoods of processes are retained between C. elegans and P. pacificus, including subtle aspects of process morphology.
source: Relative neighborhoods of processes are retained, including a number of remarkably subtle aspects of process morphology, such as the highly unique and characteristic neighborhood change of the AIB processes or the humped axon morphology of AIY at a specific location.
evidence: Supported by direct observation from TEM reconstructions

claim: These findings strongly suggest the existence of constraints in patterning of the nervous system, particularly during the phase of axonal and dendritic outgrowth.
source: These findings strongly suggest the existence of constraints in patterning of the nervous system, particularly during the phase of axonal and dendritic outgrowth, that is relative placement of processes into specific neighborhoods.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of conserved process positioning

claim: Relative placement of processes into specific neighborhoods is a critical pre-requisite for proper synaptic targeting choice by constraining which possible targets any given neuron can innervate.
source: Such placement is a critical pre-requisite for proper synaptic targeting choice by constraining which possible targets any given neuron can innervate (White, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to published theoretical framework

claim: Alterations in en passant synaptic connectivity between adjacent neurons, rather than initial patterning of neuronal fascicles, are a key substrate of evolutionary change.
source: In any case, our results argue that alterations in en passant synaptic connectivity between adjacent neurons, rather than initial patterning of neuronal fascicles, are a key substrate of evolutionary change.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that adjacency is conserved but connectivity differs

claim: Species-specific differences in olfactory behavior in insects are achieved by differences in the axonal targeting properties of olfactory sensory and projection neurons.
source: This is in striking contrast to evolutionary novelties in the olfactory systems of insects, where species-specific differences in olfactory behavior are achieved (among other mechanisms) by differences in the axonal targeting properties of olfactory sensory and projection neurons (Ramdya and Benton, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on insect olfactory systems

claim: The main drivers of chemotaxis differences between C. elegans and P. pacificus may be changes in olfactory perception rather than the means by which chemosensory signals are processed.
source: Perhaps the main drivers of these chemotaxis differences are changes in olfactory perception, that is sensory anatomy and sensory receptors, rather than the means by which chemosensory signals are processed.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observed conservation of processing circuitry

claim: A previous comparative analysis found that homologous pharyngeal neurons display differences in synaptic connectivity between C. elegans and P. pacificus.
source: A previous comparative analysis of the pharyngeal nervous system, composed of an isolated circuit of 20 neurons, also found that homologous neurons types display differences in synaptic connectivity between C. elegans and P. pacificus (Bumbarger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published comparative study

claim: Pharyngeal neurons in C. elegans synapse onto almost all neighboring processes.
source: Currently unpublished adjacency analysis of the C. elegans pharyngeal connectome suggests that pharyngeal neurons synapse onto almost all neighboring processes (S.J.C., unpubl. data)
evidence: Supported by unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript

claim: In the somatic nervous system, synapses are made only onto a fraction of neighboring processes.
source: which is in striking contrast to the somatic nervous system where synapses are made only onto a fraction of neighboring processes (White, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to established research

claim: The C. elegans genome encodes more than 1300 olfactory-type GPCRs.
source: The C. elegans genome encodes more than 1300 olfactory-type GPCRs (Robertson, 2006; Troemel et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to published genomic analyses

claim: Many C. elegans olfactory-type GPCRs are known to be co-expressed in AWA, AWB and AWC.
source: many known to be co-expressed in AWA, AWB and AWC (Troemel et al., 1995; Vidal et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published expression studies

claim: P. pacificus exhibits an odor preference profile that has scant overlap with C. elegans.
source: Yet despite the smaller GPCR repertoire, P. pacificus exhibits an odor preference profile that has scant overlap with C. elegans (Cinkornpumin et al., 2014; Hong and Sommer, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to published behavioral studies

claim: ASE laterality arose from a bilaterally symmetric ground state.
source: In accordance with earlier suggestions (Etchberger et al., 2009; Ortiz et al., 2006), these findings indicate that ASE laterality arose from a bilaterally symmetric ground state.
evidence: Inferred from the genomic and connectivity differences and supported by citations
